title: Roadmap 3: concurrency fundamentals
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Thread states, the GIL, locks, volatile and atomics, deadlock causes and fixes, and how to read a thread dump in Java and Python.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: Which Java Thread.State does a thread have while it waits to enter a synchronized block whose monitor another thread holds?

options.text: BLOCKED
options.why: Right: BLOCKED means waiting to acquire a monitor lock.

options.text: WAITING
options.why: WAITING is for Object.wait(), join() or LockSupport.park() with no timeout.

options.text: TIMED_WAITING
options.why: That state is for sleep(ms) or waits with a timeout, not monitor contention.

options.text: RUNNABLE
options.why: RUNNABLE means running or ready to run, not queued behind a monitor.

questions.explanation: BLOCKED points to monitor contention; WAITING usually points to coordination or idle pool workers. This distinction is how you read a thread dump.

questions.prompt: A pure-Python function that loops over numbers for several seconds runs in 8 threads on an 8-core machine using the default CPython 3.12 build. What do you expect compared with one thread?

options.text: No real speedup, because only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time.
options.why: Right: the GIL serialises bytecode execution; use multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound work.

options.text: Close to an 8x speedup, because the OS schedules each thread onto its own free core.
options.why: Threads exist on separate cores, but the GIL lets only one run Python code at once.

options.text: A speedup of about 2x, because the GIL allows two threads at a time.
options.why: There is one GIL per interpreter, so only one thread runs bytecode at any moment.

options.text: A crash, because CPython forbids more threads than CPU cores.
options.why: CPython allows many more threads than cores; they simply take turns.

questions.explanation: Threads still help I/O-bound Python code, since the GIL is released while waiting on sockets and files. For CPU-bound work use processes, native extensions that release the GIL, or the optional free-threaded build.

questions.prompt: Because of the GIL, counter += 1 on a shared Python int from several threads never loses updates, so no lock is needed.

options.text: True
options.why: The GIL can switch threads between the load, add and store steps of counter += 1, so updates can be lost.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: += is a read-modify-write across several bytecodes and not atomic, so guard it with a Lock.

questions.explanation: The GIL protects interpreter internals, not your invariants. Compound operations need a threading.Lock or a queue.

questions.prompt: Calling acquire() twice on a threading.Lock from the same thread, without releasing, blocks forever, while threading.RLock lets the owning thread acquire it again.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: Lock is not reentrant, so the second acquire waits for a release that never comes; RLock counts nested acquires.

options.text: False
options.why: Lock has no owner concept, so the second acquire from the same thread blocks.

questions.explanation: Java synchronized and ReentrantLock are reentrant like RLock. Use RLock when a locked method calls another locked method on the same object.

questions.prompt: Two threads each call inc() one million times on a shared field declared volatile int count, where inc() does count++. What is the likely final value?

options.text: Often below 2,000,000, because count++ is a read-modify-write and volatile does not make it atomic.
options.why: Right: volatile gives visibility and ordering, but two threads can read the same value and both write back value+1.

options.text: Exactly 2,000,000, because volatile makes every read and every write of count atomic, increments included.
options.why: Individual reads and writes are atomic, but the combined increment is not.

options.text: Exactly 2,000,000, because volatile forces the two threads to run one after the other.
options.why: volatile does not serialise threads or create a critical section.

options.text: An exception, because volatile fields cannot be modified by more than one thread.
options.why: Many threads may write a volatile field; nothing throws.

questions.explanation: Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() (a CAS loop) or a lock for counters. Use volatile for simple flags where one thread writes and others read, such as a stop flag.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which are real advantages of ReentrantLock over a synchronized block?

options.text: tryLock(timeout) lets a thread give up instead of waiting indefinitely.
options.why: Right: synchronized has no way to time out or back off while waiting for a monitor.

options.text: lockInterruptibly() allows a waiting thread to be interrupted.
options.why: Right: a thread blocked entering synchronized cannot be interrupted.

options.text: One lock can create several Condition objects, such as notFull and notEmpty.
options.why: Right: synchronized offers a single wait set per monitor.

options.text: It releases the lock automatically when an exception leaves the block.
options.why: That is synchronized; with ReentrantLock you must call unlock() in finally.

options.text: It is always faster than synchronized under any level of contention.
options.why: Modern JVMs optimise synchronized heavily; there is no guarantee either way.

questions.explanation: Choose synchronized for simple critical sections and ReentrantLock when you need timeouts, interruptibility, fairness or multiple conditions. ReadWriteLock helps read-heavy data.

options.text: Always lock the two accounts in a fixed global order, such as by account id.
options.why: Right: a consistent lock order removes the circular wait condition.

options.text: Declare the method synchronized so only one thread enters it at a time.
options.why: That serialises every transfer through one lock and does not address lock ordering for other code paths.

options.text: Add Thread.sleep(100) between the two lock acquisitions to stagger threads.
options.why: Sleeping only makes the deadlock less likely, not impossible.

options.text: Declare amt as volatile so both threads see the value consistently.
options.why: amt is not the problem; the circular lock wait is.

questions.explanation: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Break one: ordering locks, tryLock with timeouts, or using a single coarser lock.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about reading a Java thread dump (jstack) are true?

options.text: A BLOCKED thread shows waiting to lock a monitor that another thread holds.
options.why: Right: follow the lock address to find the holder and what it is doing.

options.text: jstack reports "Found one Java-level deadlock" when it detects a cycle of locks.
options.why: Right: it lists each thread and the lock it holds and wants.

options.text: Idle pool workers parked on a queue show WAITING, which is normal.
options.why: Right: workers waiting in LinkedBlockingQueue.take() are WAITING and not a problem.

options.text: Many BLOCKED threads always means the garbage collector is failing.
options.why: BLOCKED indicates lock contention; GC problems appear as long pauses.

options.text: A thread in Object.wait() keeps holding the monitor it is waiting on.
options.why: wait() releases that monitor until the thread is notified and reacquires it.

questions.explanation: Take several dumps a few seconds apart: threads stuck on the same stack are the clue. Many BLOCKED threads on one lock point to contention; a cycle points to deadlock.
